title.en: Papik, Who Killed His Wife's Brother

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother', eBook #28932

summary.en: Envious because his wife's brother Ailaq always harpoons the seals, Papik kills him silently; Ailaq's old mother vows to eat him alive and, preparing to die, lets the tide cover her on the shore. As a ghost in her bearskin coverlet she comes over the ice as a monster no dog will bark at, spreads fog and terror — a fatherless boy marked with blood nearly dies as food for the monster — until an old woman's taunt, 'There is your cousin — bark at him!', looses the dogs. Under the coverlet: human bones. Papik is found hacked in every part, and the fathers' tale teaches that murder is punished by fear itself.
summary.zh: 因內兄阿拉克每獵必中，帕皮克妒而生恨，無聲殺之。阿拉克老母立誓要生吞他，伏坐岸邊任潮水淹沒。其魂裹著熊皮罩毯化為怪物，踏冰而來，群犬噤聲、濃霧迷漫——無父男孩染血幾成怪物之食——直至老嫗一句『那是你表親，叫吧！』解開犬的咒縛。熊皮之下，竟是人骨。帕皮克被尋獲時遍體殘破，五官盡失——老嫗為子報仇。族中故老相傳：無故殺人者，必為畏懼本身所誅。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; graphic vengeance detail recorded as told in the source.

passages.text: Papik's custom was to go hunting with his wife's brother Ailaq; but whenever the two went out together, it was always Ailaq who came home with seal in tow while Papik returned empty-handed, and day by day his envy grew. Then one day Ailaq did not return at all, and Papik was silent at his home-coming. Late that evening Ailaq's old mother spoke: 'You have killed Ailaq.' 'No, I did not kill him.' Then the old woman rose and cried: 'You killed him, and said no word. The day shall yet come when I will eat you alive, for you killed Ailaq, you and no other.' She made ready to die — for as a ghost she meant to avenge her son — took her bearskin coverlet, went down to the shore close by the water, and let the tide come up and cover her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: For a long time Papik did not dare go out hunting; at last he began again. One day two men stood out on the ice by the breathing holes and heard the snow creaking with the sound of a cry, moving towards Papik, who stood a little apart; a fog came down over the ice, and then fury-shouting and fear-screaming — the monster had fallen upon Papik to devour him. Fleeing in to land they met sledges of hunters setting out and urged them back lest they be slain by fear too. At the village all crowded into one house, struggling so hard that a fatherless boy was thrust into a tub of blood, and wherever he went the snow was marked with blood: 'Now we are already made food for that monster, since that wretched boy marks out the way with a trail of blood.' Someone said let us kill him; but the others took pity and let him live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The evil spirit came in sight out on the ice, the tips of its ears showing over the hummocks as it crept along; when it came up to the houses, not a dog barked, and none dared surround it, for it was not a real bear. At last an old woman cried to the dogs: 'See, there is your cousin — bark at him!' The dogs were loosed from the magic that bound them, the men dashed forward and harpooned the thing — and cutting it up, they knew its skin for the old woman's coverlet, and its bones were human bones. The sledges that drove out to the abandoned gear found everything torn to pieces, and Papik cut about in every part: eyes, nose, mouth, and ears hacked away, the scalp torn from his head. Thus the old woman took vengeance for her son Ailaq. So the fathers used to tell: when any man killed his fellow without good cause, a monster would come and strike him dead with fear, and leave no part whole in all his body. The people of old times thought it an ill thing for men to kill each other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.

region.en: Kugkat / Natsivilik, Smith Sound, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭庫卡特與納齊維利克（史密斯海峽）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle', eBook #28932

summary.en: Fonder of his uncle's beautiful wife than of his own, Patussorssuaq kills the uncle at the ice edge rather than see the couple depart, then takes the widow. His own wife flees barefoot over the hills, hood-loose inland folk running past her on the way. Little joy follows: the widow dies soon, and at Natsivilik a fox — the soul of dead Alataq, whose amulet was a fox — snaps playfully at his coat-fringe before the ghost comes as a bear and bites him limb from limb, calling down forgetfulness on the daughter who tried to tell.
summary.zh: 帕圖舒亞克愛叔父的美妻勝過己妻；叔父攜妻遠行獵途中，他在冰邊將叔父殺害，占其寡婦。己妻光腳翻山逃回娘家，途中見內陸人披髮奔逃。得手的美妻不久病死；夏日集會時，一隻狐狸——亡叔阿拉克的魂魄（其護身符本是狐）——戲咬他的衣邊，隨後化作熊影將他啃噬得四分五裂；想報信的女兒被咒術奪去記憶，想起來時已太遲。殺人者必遭報。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; killing and ghost-vengeance presented as told in the source.

passages.text: At Kugkat lived a very beautiful woman whose husband was Alataq; at the same place lived Patussorssuaq, Alataq's nephew, who had a wife of his own but was yet fonder of his uncle's wife. One spring day Alataq made up to go out on a long hunting journey, taking his wife with him. Standing at the edge of the ice, ready to start, they were joined by Patussorssuaq — 'Are you going away?' 'Yes, both of us' — and at these words he fell upon his uncle and killed him at once, for he could not bear to see the woman go away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Patussorssuaq's wife snatched up her needle and sewing ring and fled, following the shadow of the tent over the hills to her parents, without even time for her skin stockings, her feet growing sore on the ground; on her way she saw people running with their hoods loose on their heads, as the inland folk do, but they fled away from her. The murderer went back to his own tent meaning to kill his own wife, already weary of her, but she was gone; the terrified boy inside lied that he had seen nothing. Patussorssuaq then took Alataq's widow and lived with her — but after a little time she died, and thus he had but little joy of the woman he had won by misdeed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the beginning of summer, many people were gathered at Natsivilik, Patussorssuaq among them. Out hunting, he was snapped at by a fox that caught the fringe of his coat; striking at it and missing, he thought it a common fox — but it was the soul of dead Alataq, playing with him a little before killing him outright, for Alataq's amulet was a fox. A little after, he was bitten to death by the ghost of Alataq coming upon him in the shape of a bear. His daughter heard the cries and hurried in to tell — but just as she came into the house she had quite forgotten all she wished to say, the vengeful spirit having called down forgetfulness upon her by magic means; when she remembered, it was too late. They found Patussorssuaq torn limb from limb; he had defended himself with great pieces of ice, as they could see, but all in vain. Thus punishment falls upon the man who kills.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The men who changed wives', eBook #28932

summary.en: Talilarssuaq the mischief-maker frightens the wife he has borrowed by stabbing a knife through the bench-skins; her husband Navssarssuaq dresses in his best, drags the jester out, and stabs him — 'You might at least have waited till I had dressed' — casting him on the rubbish heap. To his own wife, running to meet him, he says no, he will not murder her too, for their youngest boy is not yet grown big enough to be without her. But an avenging spirit begins to catch at him, and when sickness later kills him, it is thus spared the tearing of the ghost.
summary.zh: 頑童塔利拉舒亞克借得他人之妻，竟以刀穿凳皮嚇人；其夫納瓦舒亞克一言不發，盛裝執刃而來，拖他下凳刺死——『你好歹等我穿好衣裳』——屍棄垃圾堆。歸途遇己妻問是否也殺她，他低聲道：不，幼子保盧納還小，離不開你。此後有復仇之靈時時抓住他；待瘟疫奪其性命，那靈便無從撕裂他。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Wife-exchange described as the source community's custom of its era.

passages.text: There were once two men, Talilarssuaq and Navssarssuaq, and they changed wives. Talilarssuaq was a mischievous fellow, given to frightening people. One evening, sitting in the house with the other's wife, whom he had borrowed, he thrust his knife suddenly through the skins of the bench; the woman ran to her husband: 'Go in and kill Talilarssuaq; he is playing very dangerous tricks.' Navssarssuaq rose without a word, put on his best clothes, took his knife, went straight up to Talilarssuaq — now lying on the bench talking to himself — pulled him out on the floor and stabbed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The men who changed wives'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'You might at least have waited till I had dressed,' said Talilarssuaq; but Navssarssuaq hauled him out through the passage way, cast him on the rubbish heap, and went his way saying nothing. On the way he met his wife, who asked: 'Are you not going to murder me, too?' 'No,' he answered in a deep voice, 'for Pualuna is not yet grown big enough to be without you' — Pualuna being their youngest son. Some time after that deed he began to perceive that he was haunted: 'There is some invisible thing which now and again catches hold of me,' he told his comrades. It was the avenging spirit, watching him. About that time many in the place fell sick, and among them Navssarssuaq; the sickness killed him, and thus the avenging spirit was not able to tear him in pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The men who changed wives'; not verbatim.

title.en: Artuk, Who Did All Forbidden Things

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden', eBook #28932

summary.en: Having buried his wife, Artuk refuses to observe the mourning taboos — he hacks frozen meat with a stone axe, shakes out his inner coat on the ice, drinks sun-melted water on an iceberg — declaring it all lies, in scorn of his fellows' beliefs. Fear comes upon him the day he drives out; he binds his unwilling son to the sledge uprights and never returns alive. That evening his daughter hears two spirits laughing mockingly in the air; the sledges find Artuk torn to pieces far out on the ice, the untouched son dead of fright beside him.
summary.zh: 妻子下葬後，阿爾圖克拒守喪禁——以石斧砍凍肉、在冰上抖內衣、登冰山飲日融之水——斥舊俗為謊，蔑視族人信仰。一日驅犬出行，恐懼襲來，他將不肯同行的兒子縛上雪橇立柱，竟一去不返。當晚女兒聽見空中兩靈竊笑——那是父親遭報的信號。次日雪橇四出，在遠冰上尋見他：已被撕為碎片，如歷來冒犯祖俗者一般；縛在橇上的兒子分毫未傷，卻活活嚇死。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Mourning taboos are core Inuit ritual law; the tale is the tradition's own enforcement narrative.

passages.text: A man whose name was Artuk had buried his wife, but refused to remain aloof from the doings which those who have been busied with the dead are forbidden to share, saying he did not hold by such old customs. Some fellow-villagers were cutting up frozen meat for food; after watching them work at the meat with their knives for a while, he took a stone axe and hacked at it, saying 'That is the way to cut up meat' — and this although it was forbidden. The same day he went out on the ice and took off his inner coat to shake it, though that was forbidden; and he went up on to an iceberg and drank water the sun had melted there, knowing well this too was forbidden. All these things he did in scorn of what his fellows believed, for he said it was all lies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But one day, starting out with his sledge, fear came upon him and he dared not go alone; his son would not go with him willingly, so he took him and bound him to the uprights of the sledge, and carried him so. He never returned alive. Late in the evening his daughter heard in the air the mocking laughter of two spirits, and knew at once they laughed so that she might know how her father had been punished for his ill-doing. Next day many sledges went out to search, and found Artuk far out on the ice, torn to pieces, as is the way with those whom the spirits have punished for refusing to observe the customs of their forefathers. The son, bound to the sledge, had not been touched — but he had died of fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Thunder Spirits: Two Sisters of the Mountain

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The thunder spirits', eBook #28932

summary.en: Scolded once too often for their noise, two sisters run away with only a dogskin, a piece of boot skin, and a fire stone, and build a house on a high mountain, refusing ever to return. When they must die of hunger they turn into evil spirits and become thunder: shaking the dried boot skin raises the south-westerly gales, striking the fire stone lights great fire in the heavens, and their tears pour down as rain. Returning to frighten men to death — sparing only a child-back-carrying woman to tell of it — they fear one thing alone: the blood of a cut red dog, led dripping round the house.
summary.zh: 兩姊妹厭父親斥責，攜犬皮、靴皮與火石上山築屋，拒不歸家。饑餓將死之際化為惡靈，成為雷霆：抖動乾靴皮則西南狂風驟起，擊打火石則天際烈焰，落淚則大雨傾盆。她們重返人間嚇死多人，獨留一名背孩子的婦人傳述其可怖。雷霆唯懼一物——割耳放血的黑狗，血繞屋滴灑，屋便不著火。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Thunder etiology and the red-dog protective rite are documented as living practice in the source.

passages.text: Two sisters were playing together, and their father, who had but few children and was not wont to hear any kind of noise, could not bear the sound; at last he began to scold them, telling them to take their playing farther away. When the girls grew up and began to understand things, they desired to run away on account of the scolding, and set out taking with them only a little dogskin, a piece of boot skin, and a fire stone, going up into a high mountain to build themselves a house. Their father and mother searched for them in vain, for the girls kept hiding themselves; they had grown to be true mountain dwellers, keeping far from the places of men. Only the reindeer hunters saw them now and again, and the girls always refused to go back to their kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When at last the time came that they must die of hunger, they turned into evil spirits and became thunder. When they shake their dried boot skin, the gales come up, the south-westerly gales; great fire is seen in the heavens whenever they strike their fire stone, and the rain pours down whenever they shed tears. Their father held many spirit callings hoping to make them return, and ceased only when he found they were dead. But after the girls had become spirits, they came back to the places of men, frightening many to death — first of all their own father and mother, because of the trouble they had made. The only one they did not kill was a woman bearing a child on her back, and her they let live, that she might tell how terrible they were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the thunder spirits come, even the earth itself is stricken with terror: stones which lie on level ground, not on any slope at all, roll in fear towards men. The thunder comes with the south-westerly gales; there is a noise and crackling in the air as of dry skins shaken, the sky glows from time to time with fire from their firestone, and great rocks and everything which stands up high in the air begin to glow. When this happens, men take out a red dog and cut its ear until the blood comes, then lead the beast round about the house, letting the blood drip everywhere, for then the house will not take fire. A red dog was the only thing those girls who were turned to thunder feared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.

title.en: Nerrivik, Ruler of the Sea Creatures
title.zh: 涅里維克：海洋眾獸之主

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Nerrivik', eBook #28932

summary.en: A bird-man courts and marries a woman, catching fish he calls seal; when he loses his walrus-tusk spectacles she sees his bad eyes and weeps at his ugliness, and her visiting brothers carry her home. The bird-husband raises a storm with his wings to reclaim her, and the frightened crew, judging her the storm's cause, throw her into the sea — her grandfather cutting off the hand that grasped the boat. Drowned, she becomes Nerrivik, ruler over all the creatures of the sea; with but one hand she cannot comb her hair, and when men catch no seal the wizards go down to comb it, and she sends seal and other creatures forth by way of thanks.
summary.zh: 鳥人假扮男子娶得妻子，捕魚而稱之為海豹；丟了海象牙眼鏡後，妻子看清他的醜眼而泣。探望的兄弟們將她帶回。鳥夫以巨翅搧起風暴索妻，驚惶的舟人把災因推向她，將她拋入海中——抓住船舷的手被祖父一劍砍斷。溺斃的她沉入海底，成為統御海中眾獸的涅里維克：獨手難梳長髮，漁獲不至時，巫師下海為她梳髮，她便遣出海豹群獸以為回報。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo sea-ruler myth recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Nerrivik is the Smith Sound name of the sea-mother, cognate with Sedna of the Central Eskimo; cross-ref sedna-sea-mother.

passages.text: A bird once wished to marry a woman: he got himself a fine sealskin coat, and having weak eyes made spectacles out of a walrus tusk, greatly set upon looking as nice as possible. Then he set off in the shape of a man, came to a village, took a wife, and brought her home, going out thereafter to catch fish, which he called seal, and brought to her. Once he lost his spectacles, and his wife, seeing his bad eyes, burst out weeping because he was so ugly — but her husband only laughed: 'Oho, so you saw my eyes? Hahaha!' And he put on his spectacles again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Her brothers, longing for their sister, came out one day to visit her, and while her husband was out hunting they took her away with them. The husband, coming home to find her gone, set out in pursuit — swinging his wings with mighty force and raising a violent storm, for he was a great wizard. The boat began to take in water, the wind grew fiercer as he doubled the beating of his wings, the waves rose white with foam, and when those in the boat began to suspect that the woman was the cause of the storm, they took her up and cast her into the sea. She tried to grasp the side of the boat, and her grandfather sprang up and cut off her hand — and so she was drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the bottom of the sea she became Nerrivik, ruler over all the creatures in the sea. When men catch no seal, the wizards go down to Nerrivik: having but one hand, she cannot comb her hair, and this they do for her, and she, by way of thanks, sends seal and other creatures forth to men. Men call her Nerrivik because she gives them food. That is the story of the ruler of the sea — the Smith Sound telling of the one-handed sea-mother, sister-tale to the Sedna of the Central Eskimo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The wife who lied', eBook #28932

summary.en: Navaranapaluk, a man-eater's daughter married into a peaceful tribe, goes visiting in midwinter wearing mittens on her feet to fake mistreatment; her pitying kinsfolk make war, slay the village's women while the men are away, and hoist the bodies on poles. The three escaped women plait arrow-sinew until the naked bone shows on their fingers; the avengers hide among rocks behind the enemies' houses, betrayed — and destroyed — by one barking dog on the roof. The widows are carried off; Navaranapaluk, seized by two men together, has both arms cut through, and dies for having lied.
summary.zh: 食人族之女嫁入和平部落，訪親途中以襪代靴，偽稱受虐；族人憐憫興兵，趁男獵女守之際屠戮全村婦女，屍懸長杆。三名倖存女子捻製箭弦，捻至指骨外露；復仇者伏於敵屋後岩間，卻因屋頂一犬吠聲而敗露——敵眾盡歿，寡婦被擄。撒謊的納瓦拉納帕盧克被兩名男子同時拖走，雙臂被刀切斷，血盡而亡——此乃她撒謊的報應。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Graphic massacre and mutilation presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: Navaranapaluk came of a tribe of man-eaters, but when she grew up she was taken to wife by one of a tribe that did not eat men. Once, going off on a visit to her own people, she put mittens on her feet instead of boots, to make it appear that her husband's people had dealt ill by her. It was midwinter, and her kinsfolk pitied her greatly when they saw her come thus, and agreed to make war against the tribe her husband belonged to. They set out and came to that village at a time when all the men were away and only the women at home; these they took and slew, and only three escaped — one covered with the skin she was dressing, one hidden in the box for dog's meat, and one crept into a store shed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the men came home they found all their womenfolk killed, the more angered that the slayers had hoisted the bodies on long poles with the points stuck through them, and thought at once of Navaranapaluk, who had fled. They fell to making ready for war, preparing arrows in great numbers; the three women who were left alive plaited sinew thread to fix the points, working so eagerly that at last no more flesh was left on their fingers, and the naked bone showed through. Coming up behind the enemies' houses, they hid themselves among great rocks. The slayers, who had kept watch since their return, believing the avengers would not fail to come, took turns watching; then one old woman among them dreamed that two creatures were fighting above her head, and the household gathered to ask counsel of the spirits — when suddenly a dog on the roof of the house began to bark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The men dashed out, but their enemies had already surrounded the house, and shot down every man with arrows until there were no more left; then they chose themselves wives from among the widows and bore them off. But two of them took Navaranapaluk and hurried off with her, and she — thinking both wished to have her to wife — cried out, 'Which is it to be? Which is it to be?' The men laughed and made no answer, but ran on with her; then suddenly they cut through both her arms with their knives. Soon she fell, the blood went from her, and she died. This fate they meted out to her because she lied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.
